title: What Must Leadership Decide, and When?
say: Welcome. This is the executive briefing for Book 00 of the Federal Modernization Workbook, Orientation and Program. It runs about thirty minutes, and it's for the people who sponsor, fund and answer for modernization: executive sponsors, CIOs, CISOs and program executives. One point up front. The workbook is independent technical guidance, not federal policy. Where it says a law or directive requires something, it cites the source. The phases, gates, principles and decision rights are the workbook's own recommendation: one way to meet those requirements, not a requirement itself. The argument is short. For twenty years Active Directory quietly did governance nobody wrote down. Federal policy and vendor support dates now set clocks the estate can't ignore. Meeting them one product at a time rebuilds the same gaps somewhere new, so modernization has to run as one governed program. I'll cover why now, what the program is, who decides, and how it runs. Every decision slide names the decision, its owner, and when it's needed. Let's start with why.

title: The directory governed the estate, and nobody wrote it down
say: Start with why. Most federal estates still run the client/server model they built in the early 2000s, with an Active Directory forest at the center. Placing a user or a computer in the tree decided, all at once and with no separate record, who administers it, which Group Policy applies, what its groups can reach, how it's named in DNS, and which certificates it receives. Agencies got governance as a side effect of running a directory. The cost is that it was never written down. The cloud doesn't inherit it. Entra ID's administrative units can't be nested, and Intune applies policy to groups with no hierarchy, where two policies that disagree produce a conflict, not an inheritance rule. So every replacement needs someone to decide what the old placement meant. Retire the forest without recovering those decisions, and you don't modernize your governance. You delete it. The first decision is the sponsor's, when the charter is signed: treat this as governance reconstruction, not only a technical migration. Next, the dates that make it urgent.

title: Federal policy now sets the dates
say: The second reason is the schedule, and the first set of clocks is federal policy. M-22-09 set Zero Trust objectives for the end of fiscal 2024. That date has passed, but the actions remain in force. CISA's BOD 25-01 set mandatory cloud tenant configurations, with the policies due June 20, 2025. BOD 26-02 directs agencies to remove internet-facing end-of-support edge devices, the listed ones by February 5, 2027. FedRAMP's Consolidated Rules for 2026 take mandatory effect on January 1, 2027, and FedRAMP accepts no new Rev5 certification applications after June 11, 2027. The one that needs attention first is logging. OMB M-26-14 rescinded M-21-31, and its deadlines count from CISA's Logging Reference Architecture, published August 20, 2026. Counted from that date, the Agency Logging Plan falls on November 18 of this year. That's the program's arithmetic, not a date OMB published. So the nearest decision: the CISO's office confirms those dates, starting with the logging plan. Next, the vendor clocks.

title: Vendor support dates cluster on the same estate
say: The second set of clocks is vendor support. After end of support there are no new security updates and no assisted support, and for an estate built in the early 2000s, the dates cluster. Windows 10 and Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 ended in October 2025. SQL Server 2016, SharePoint Server 2016 and 2019, and the last Windows Server 2012 updates ended this year. The one to watch is Windows Server 2016, which ends on January 12, 2027, under three months away. It runs many of the domain controllers built in the last decade. And Microsoft Identity Manager 2016 ends on January 9, 2029, so an agency syncing HR data through it has a date, not an open-ended bridge. A vendor date isn't a federal mandate on its own, but the two connect. BOD 26-02 turns end of support into a directed action for edge devices, and every security plan promises flaw remediation an unsupported product can't deliver. So running past end of support is a decision for the authorizing official, who signs the risk acceptance. The first falls due on January 12. Next, how to read these clocks.

title: Read the clocks exactly, then run one program
say: The clocks are often quoted for more than they say, so read them exactly. FedRAMP certifies cloud services, and each agency still authorizes its own systems. Moderate is now a certification class: Class C includes the current Moderate baseline. No federal document requires a Zero Trust maturity stage. And BOD 25-01 covers production cloud tenants, not on-premises Active Directory. Nothing makes the estate fail on a single date. It's surrounded by deadlines, each binding a different part of it, and each assuming the agency knows what it runs, who owns it and what governs it. That's why this can't be a set of projects. Moving devices to Intune needs the policy carried over; Conditional Access needs the access groups carried over. Separate projects rediscover those decisions differently, or not at all. A program can sequence the work against the dates; a collection of projects can only race them. So the decision for the sponsor and CIO, before the budget lines are set: fund and govern this as one sequenced program, with one dependency chain and one set of gates. Next, what that program is.

title: The charter: the page the sponsor signs
say: Now, what the program is. It starts with a short charter: the page the sponsor signs, and the page every later decision is checked against. Is this in scope, does it serve an objective, does it move a success criterion? The charter names the costs it sets out to remove: migration risk hidden in dependencies, drift between intended and actual state, weak evidence of change, and the expense of reconciling fragmented stores. Against those it sets six objectives. At their heart is one authoritative origin for organizational structure and identity attributes, with every other copy derived, and governance rebuilt explicitly instead of inherited. Change runs in controlled waves that close with evidence, without rip-and-replace. The scope is deliberate. The program feeds compliance frameworks rather than replacing them. Identity providers, networks and device managers stay the enforcers. And the agency executes its own cutover. The decision: the sponsor signs the charter and puts names in its governance table, starting with the sponsor and the steward, as Phase 0's entry work. Next, how the charter's success gets tested.

title: Six success criteria, each tested at a gate
say: A sponsor can't sign off an outcome with no test. So the charter turns each of its six success criteria into a measure, the evidence that shows it, and the gate where it's checked. A few examples. The current-state assessment covers every forest in scope, with zero open priority-one findings, checked at G0. Every attribute that drives access has exactly one designated source, checked at G1. The pilot division clears G2 with zero drift for a hold period; fourteen days is the illustrative example. And drift detection is itself watched: a missed run is a halt condition. The numbers are illustrative defaults. The agency sets its own, records them, and doesn't change them silently. And the criteria stop at the pilot on purpose. The sixth criterion is the sponsor's own: leadership can describe the path, the risks and the measures without citing internal decision records. The sponsor answers yes to each pre-start question by G0, and the steering committee reviews the drift trend monthly. Next, the principles underneath.

title: Fifteen principles, one idea underneath
say: The charter's principles expand to fifteen, but one idea runs under all of them. Keep the record of what should be true apart from the systems that enforce it, and make every change prove itself against that record. In practice, every claim has one authoritative origin. Every change starts from that source, carries an authoritative authorization, runs with just-in-time least privilege, and closes with provenance and evidence. No closure counts unless it carries its proof. And drift detection re-checks on a schedule. One rule deserves an executive's attention. The program replaces the OU tree with attributes, and a user with an empty attribute falls out of the dynamic group, and so out of every policy that targets it. Attribute completeness is a security control. The decision here is the steward's, and it comes before the first change is made: set the evidence and provenance expectations every later change must meet. Next, the phases and gates.

title: Seven phases, six gates, and who clears each
say: A plan earns its keep by saying what has to be true before the next step starts, not by putting dates on a chart. Book 01 sets seven phases and six gates: pre-flight, foundation, a pilot division, general rollout, legacy retirement, retirement of AD DS itself, and then steady state, which runs indefinitely. The gates are owned in proportion to what they end. The steward clears G0, G1 and G4, and co-signs the pilot gate with the executive sponsor. The sponsor and steering committee clear rollout. The sponsor and CIO clear the retirement of AD DS. Here's the budget catch. The program's master plan sequences 48 milestones over an illustrative 52 weeks, but its cutover ends with AD DS still running. And Book 01's 52-week model assumes a mid-size, clean forest; large federal estates typically run multi-year. So the decision for the sponsor and CIO, when they accept the plan: budget the AD DS retirement phase on top of those 52 weeks. Next, the workstreams inside the phases.

title: Five workstreams in parallel, one critical path
say: Five workstreams carry the work: identity, policy, services, compute and access. They run together, because finishing one before starting the next roughly doubles the program. They still have an order. Identity comes first, because policy, access, devices and data all decide based on who or what is asking. Policy follows identity. Services, naming and addressing, can run in parallel. Compute comes mid to late, and access comes later, because it consumes both identity and policy. The master plan organized the same work as five technology pillars, and that left two gaps: nobody owned the question of which policy surface owns a setting, and access had no pillar at all. Book 01 closes them, with a security-engineering lead for policy and a joint identity and security lead for access. Every week lost in assessment or attribute design moves every later gate, and one dependency never relaxes: PKI waits for identity. The decision, during Phase 0: name the five workstream leads, including those two. Next, the projects.

title: Seven projects, run inside the program
say: Seven projects turn the program's most common gaps into executable work, each with its own sponsor, lead and pilot. They cover identity lifecycle, devices, network and access, continuous monitoring and evidence, privileged access, data platforms, and the software supply chain. The suggested order matters. Identity goes first, because everything else consumes its attributes and owners; a device project started on unreliable attributes produces policy bypass. Privileged access is chartered fifth but isn't fifth in practice, because the Foundation gate already needs emergency access accounts vaulted and tested. Every charter asks for a working pilot, not a finished estate. Two rules keep the portfolio coherent. No project designates a second authoritative source for something another project owns. And every project emits evidence in the shape the monitoring project defines. The projects aren't a second governance structure. No project clears a program gate on its own, and every project lead reports to the steward. Next, who decides.

title: Who decides: one decider per row
say: Who decides? The book's advice: name the people allowed to say no, give each decision one of them, and make the repository remember who said yes. The executive sponsor, with the CIO, owns scope, funding and sequence, breaks ties, and decides when Active Directory components retire. The CISO sets the control requirements every target surface must meet. The authorizing official is the only official who can accept security and privacy risk. The steward leads the program office and owns the plan and the repository. HR decides what each organizational attribute means. And workstream leads own their designs, inside the CISO's requirements. Federal requirements already name some of these people. M-22-09 required a zero trust implementation lead, and M-19-17 requires an agency-wide ICAM governance structure. So the decision for the sponsor and CIO, in Phase 0: name the sponsor, the steward and the steering committee, and build them from those existing roles, not alongside them. Next, three decisions the plans put on the wrong desk.

title: Three decisions the plans put on the wrong desk
say: Most of what the program's plans said about decisions holds. Three items don't. Residual risk first. The plans let the security lead and the steward accept it jointly. Under the Risk Management Framework, only the authorizing official can. The others prepare and recommend, and the acceptance carries a justification, compensating controls and an end date. Second, budget and licenses belong to the sponsor and CIO, who own funding; the steward prepares the case. Third, the master plan made the steward the sole signatory at every gate. Book 01 spreads the gates across the steward, the sponsor, the steering committee and the CIO. A few separations keep the governance honest. The authorizing official is a government official, and the decision can't be delegated: contractors can prepare a risk acceptance, but can't sign one. And requesters don't approve their own changes. So from G0 onward, every risk acceptance comes from the authorizing official in writing, with an end date. Next, the people and the rhythm.

title: The people the program needs, and its rhythm
say: Who does the work? The master plan estimated the program office and workstreams at about five and a half full-time equivalents for an illustrative 52-week program. It's a planning model, not a staffing standard. What matters more is what the estimate leaves out: application owners for every application that moves, help desk capacity for every wave, HR and contractor-source owners, records and privacy, and the CISO's and authorizing official's time for risk decisions. The program can't run without them, so budget for them explicitly, and cross-train two people per workstream. The rhythm is simple. A weekly report rates each workstream green, yellow or red. The steering committee meets every two weeks, gate readiness is reviewed monthly, and each gate review ends in go, no-go or conditional go. Two consecutive red weeks for any workstream go to the sponsor. The decision for the sponsor and CIO: put those people in the Phase 0 business case, alongside the licenses, and approve the budget before design begins. Now, how the program runs.

title: Pre-flight: assessment before action
say: It starts with pre-flight, and one rule: assessment before action. No migration work starts until the whole forest is inventoried, classified and committed to the repository, and every plan is generated from that data. First, the program builds the place where every decision gets written down: a platform host with one authoritative, protected writer. It's a Tier 0 system, and a branch protection the steward can quietly override is a convention, not a control. Then it reads the estate, read-only first, and the phase delivers twenty-three artifacts, fifteen of them committed before G0. G0 has three conditions: the platform host is operational, the assessment is committed, and no priority-one finding is open. Every finding is classed Critical, High, Medium or Low, and each class has a gate that closes it. The decision point is the Critical finding. It's remediated before G0, or formally accepted by the authorizing official, and the steward clears G0 on that basis. Next, foundation and pilot.

title: Foundation and pilot: prove it on one division
say: Phase 1, Foundation, generates the plans from the committed assessment and designs every surface from them: attributes, dynamic groups, Intune policy, Conditional Access, sync, DNS and PKI. One planning note: group processing is planned in hours, not minutes. The steward clears G1 when the designs are approved, the baseline Conditional Access policies are enforced after at least a week in report-only, the emergency access accounts are vaulted and tested, the HR feed is live, and every High finding is remediated. Phase 2 proves the whole pattern on real people: one division, typically IT, which tolerates disruption best. It's measured against eight criteria, from sign-in success to help desk volume. Set the thresholds in the decision log before the pilot opens, and judge them from the systems, not from opinion. Every surface has a rollback trigger. G2 is signed jointly by the steward and the executive sponsor: zero drift for the agreed hold period, every criterion met, and no hybrid-joined PC without a cut date. Next, rollout and retirement.

title: Roll out in waves, then retire only what nothing uses
say: Phase 3 repeats the proven pattern in waves until every division has moved, usually by region, lowest-risk region first. Group Policy links stay in place during a wave, and come off only after seven days of clean compliance. The sponsor and steering committee clear G3 when every division has passed its own exit gate. Then the work changes character: these phases take old things away. Phase 4 retires legacy pieces such as AD FS, DNS forwarders, Group Policy links and legacy servers, each through its own plan, and only while its rollback still works. The steward clears G4. Phase 5 retires AD DS itself, which the master plan never reached, or reduces it to a documented Kerberos island with an end date. Two steps are easy to forget. Records come before hardware. And because domain controllers store every account's password hash, retired hosts and their storage are sanitized. The sponsor and CIO clear G5, and decide when each component retires, after the records officer is consulted. Next, steady state.

title: Steady state, and what success looks like
say: Phase 6, steady state, has no exit gate. The modernized estate runs under continuous governance: drift detection daily, reassessment weekly, a monthly compliance report, quarterly access reviews and an annual architecture review. The finish line is zero drift findings and signed evidence flowing to the SIEM. Every finding gets a severity, and every severity a clock. The master plan's defaults run from four hours for a Critical finding to thirty days for a Low one. The agency sets its own values; what the program insists on is that there are some, written into its continuous monitoring strategy and measured. Success is measured twice. Delivery measures turn green gate by gate. Outcome measures are what operations keeps green after the project ends. A program can meet every delivery measure and still fail if the outcomes drift once the team leaves. That's why the handover is part of the scorecard. Before the team leaves, the steward records who owns the repository, each drift class, each severity and each review. Next, the risks.

title: The risk register: what can sink the program
say: The risk register names what can sink the program, starting with five program risks. Hidden dependencies get missed, so a structured assessment and the pilot surface unknowns early. Competing sources of truth persist, so each object class gets one authoritative origin. The organization resists making authority explicit, so decision rights get one decider per row. And tooling leads the design, which is why the target model comes first: tools bought first automate the old ambiguity faster. Beneath them sit twenty-five delivery risks, and a few deserve executive attention. Legacy applications that depend on NTLM can't be evaluated by Conditional Access, so each dependency becomes a finding with an owner and a dated exception. Strong certificate mapping isn't a future risk: domain controllers already enforce it. And governance can decay once the team leaves. The register doesn't satisfy a control, but it tells the agency when to update its security plan and risk assessment: at every gate. The authorizing official accepts residual risk, and security risk left open past a gate becomes a plan of action and milestones item. Finally, the decisions in one place.

title: Decisions to make, and who makes them
say: So, the decisions, with their owners. The executive sponsor charters the program as governance reconstruction and signs the charter as Phase 0's entry work. The sponsor and CIO fund one sequenced program, with the AD DS retirement phase and the people beyond the core team in the budget, approved before design begins. And they build the steward and steering committee from the zero trust lead and ICAM governance body the agency already has. The CISO's office confirms the M-26-14 dates, starting with the Agency Logging Plan, due November 18 by the program's count. The authorizing official decides whether anything runs past end of support, beginning with Windows Server 2016 on January 12. The steward sets the evidence expectations before the first change, clears G0 only when every Critical finding is closed or accepted, and, with the sponsor, records the pilot's thresholds before it opens. And the steward records the handover before the team leaves. None of these is a purchase. The estate's governance was never written down, the dates that bind it now belong to others, and the only way to meet them without losing that governance is to recover it deliberately, once, in one program. Thank you.
